title: The Emperor’s New Clothes
author: Hans Christian Andersen (retold)
summary: 「愚か者には見えない布」を売り込む二人のペテン師。だれも「見えない」と言えないまま、皇帝は行列に出ます。アンデルセン「はだかの王様」。

source.note: Retold in simpler English from Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Emperor’s New Clothes” (1837, public domain).

paragraphs: Many years ago there lived an emperor who loved new clothes more than anything else in the world. He did not care about his soldiers, or about the theater, or about riding in the park, unless it gave him a chance to show off his new clothes. He had a different coat for every hour of the day. In other countries, people said, “The king is in his council room.” In his country, people said, “The emperor is in his dressing room.”

The emperor lived in a large, lively city, and many visitors came there every day. One day, two strangers arrived. They told everyone they were weavers, and that they could weave the most beautiful cloth anyone could imagine. Not only were the colors and patterns wonderful, they said, but the cloth also had a magical quality. Clothes made from it were invisible to anyone who was stupid or who was not good enough for his job.

“Those would be perfect clothes!” thought the emperor. “If I wore them, I could find out which men in my kingdom are not good enough for their jobs. I could tell the wise from the foolish. I must have that cloth at once!” He gave the two men a large bag of gold so they could begin their work immediately.

The two men set up two looms and pretended to work hard. But there was nothing on the looms at all. They asked for the finest silk and the purest gold thread, and they put it all into their own bags. Then they sat at their empty looms and moved their hands until late into the night.

After a while, the emperor wanted to know how the work was going. But he felt a little uncomfortable when he remembered that a stupid person could not see the cloth. He did not really worry about himself, of course. Still, he decided to send someone else first.
“I will send my honest old minister,” he thought. “He is very clever, and nobody is better at his job than he is.”

So the good old minister went into the room where the two men were working at their empty looms. “Heaven help me!” he thought, and his eyes opened wide. “I can’t see anything at all!” But he did not say so.

The two men asked him to come closer. “Isn’t it a beautiful pattern? Aren’t the colors lovely?” They pointed to the empty looms. The poor old minister looked and looked, but he could see nothing, because there was nothing there. “Am I stupid?” he thought. “I never believed that. And nobody must know it. Am I not good enough for my job? No, I must never say that I can’t see the cloth.”
“Oh, it is beautiful! Charming!” said the minister, looking through his glasses. “What a pattern, what colors! I will tell the emperor that I like it very much.”
The two men described the colors and the pattern in detail, and the old minister listened carefully so he could repeat every word to the emperor. And he did.
Then the men asked for more money, more silk and more gold thread. They put it all in their bags, and they continued to work at the empty looms.

Soon the emperor sent another official to see the cloth. The same thing happened to him. He looked and looked, but there was nothing to see. “I am not stupid,” he thought. “So it must be that I am not right for my important job. That is strange. But nobody must find out.” So he praised the cloth he could not see, and he told the emperor, “It is magnificent!”

Everyone in the city was talking about the wonderful cloth. Finally the emperor himself wanted to see it while it was still on the loom. With a group of his finest courtiers, including the two who had already been there, he went to visit the clever weavers. They were weaving with all their might, but without a single thread.
“Isn’t it magnificent?” said the two officials. “Look, Your Majesty, what a design! What colors!” And they pointed at the empty looms, because they were sure that everyone else could see the cloth.

“What is this?” thought the emperor. “I can’t see anything! This is terrible! Am I stupid? Am I not fit to be emperor? That would be the worst thing that could happen to me.” But aloud he said, “Oh, it is very beautiful. It has my highest approval.” And he nodded and looked at the empty loom. He would never say he could see nothing.

All his courtiers looked and looked. None of them saw anything more than the others, but they all said, just like the emperor, “Oh, it is very beautiful!” And they advised him to wear clothes made from this wonderful cloth for the first time in the great procession that was coming soon.

On the night before the procession, the two men stayed up all night with more than sixteen candles burning, so everyone could see how hard they were working. They pretended to take the cloth off the loom. They cut the air with big scissors. They sewed with needles that had no thread. At last they said, “Now the emperor’s new clothes are ready!”

The emperor came with his most important courtiers. The two men held up their arms as if they were holding something. “Here are the trousers! Here is the coat! Here is the long cape!” they said. “They are as light as a spider’s web. You might think you are wearing nothing at all, but that is the beauty of it.”
“Yes,” said all the courtiers, but they could not see anything, because there was nothing to see.

“If Your Majesty would kindly take off your clothes,” said the men, “we will help you into the new ones here in front of the big mirror.” The emperor took off his clothes, and they pretended to put each new piece on him. The emperor turned around and around in front of the mirror.
“How well they fit! How beautiful they look!” everyone said. “What a pattern! What colors! They are perfect clothes!”

Then the emperor walked out into the street under a beautiful golden canopy. Two servants walked behind him, holding up the long cape with their hands in the air. They did not dare to admit that there was nothing to hold.

All the people standing in the streets and looking out of their windows said, “Oh! The emperor’s new clothes are the most beautiful he has ever had! What a wonderful cape! How perfectly it fits!” Nobody wanted others to know that he saw nothing, because that would mean he was stupid or not good at his job. None of the emperor’s clothes had ever been such a success.
“But he hasn’t got anything on!” said a little child.
“Listen to the innocent child!” said the child’s father. And one person whispered to another what the child had said. “He hasn’t got anything on. A little child says he hasn’t got anything on.”
“But he hasn’t got anything on!” all the people cried at last.

The emperor shivered, because he knew that the people were right. But he thought, “I must continue the procession until the end.” So he walked on, prouder than ever, and his servants walked behind him, holding up the cape that was not there at all.
